title: Exploitation of Remote Services
summary: Exploitation of remote services is the use of a software flaw in a network facing service to run attacker controlled code on another host, most often to move laterally inside a network that is already partly compromised. The target may be an operating system component, a file sharing service, a remote desktop service, a database listener or a management appliance, and the injected code runs with the privileges of that service. Before attacking, an adversary usually probes for a reachable service and a version that looks unpatched, which produces its own scan and enumeration traffic. Evidence appears in service logs, crash dumps, unexpected child processes spawned by a service account, authentication events from one workstation to many servers, and file or registry changes made by a process that is not the service itself. Legitimate remote administration also creates service logons, so the useful signals are timing, volume, source host and the process tree rather than the logon event alone.

beginner.definition: Remote services are programs that other computers can connect to over the network, such as file sharing or remote desktop. This technique means using a mistake in that program to run your own code. The attacker does not need a password if the mistake is serious enough. It is a common way to move from one computer to the next.
beginner.whyItMatters: One broken computer is often just the start. If a service on another machine has a known flaw, the attacker can jump across without any password. Servers are the favourite target, because they hold the data. Patching is the main defence, but you must also watch for the signs. Ignoring this lets a small incident grow into a full network breach.
howItWorks: The attacker already has a foothold on one machine inside the network.
They scan for reachable services and note the version and patch level of each.
They pick a service with a known flaw that matches what they found.
They send specially formed network data that triggers the bug in that service.
The service runs the attacker code with its own rights, often as a system account.
They repeat the process from the new machine to reach further systems.
beginner.example: Imagine a block of flats where every home has the same model of back door. One lock has a known fault, so a firm sells a key that opens it. A thief who gets into the car park can try that key on every back door in the building. Once inside one flat, they can reach the shared corridor and try the next door. Fixing every lock, not just the first one, is the only real cure.
takeaways: Remote service flaws let an attacker move between computers without stealing a password.
Patch exposed services quickly and remove any service that nobody actually needs.
Watch for services that start unusual programs or receive logons from unexpected hosts.

objectives: Explain how a flaw in a network service leads to code running on another host.
Describe the discovery steps that come before exploitation of a remote service.
Name the log sources that show service crashes, new child processes and remote logons.
Distinguish normal remote administration from lateral movement through a service.
List the patching and exposure reduction steps that lower this risk most.
